claim: Extrapolated across all 9.2 million streamers on Twitch, the Gini coefficient of streamer revenue is approximately 0.93 — a level of concentration far exceeding any national income distribution.
stance_target: Creator income is so concentrated that the median creator's earnings are effectively zero and mean-based figures are meaningless as a description of the typical creator.
scope_conditions: Derived by fitting a parabolic fractal function (y = log(x-b) - c log(x)^2 + norm; b about 0.259, c about 0.0392, norm about 15.78) to the measured top-10,000 rank-revenue curve and extending it to the full 9.2 million-streamer population reported by TwitchTracker. This is an EXTRAPOLATION from a fitted curve, not a direct measurement of the tail. Covers Amazon-paid Twitch revenue only, August 2019 - October 2021, global platform, no country breakdown.
quoted_support: Moreover, projecting the analysis to the entirety of Twitch streamers using a parabolic fractal fit reveals a much larger level of inequality (Gini approximately 0.93; Fig. 1B). This is a truly impressive value.
region: Global Twitch platform; NOT disaggregable by country, so not directly applicable to Southeast Asia

claim: Among the top 10,000 Twitch streamers by revenue, earnings over August 2019 - October 2021 ranged from USD 9,500,000 at the top down to USD 23,520 at rank 10,000.
stance_target: Even inside the elite 0.1% of creators, the top-to-bottom spread is roughly 400-fold, and the floor of the elite tier is barely a modest salary spread over more than two years.
scope_conditions: Amazon-paid Twitch revenue only — excludes sponsorships, brand deals, merchandise and all off-platform income, which other sources say exceed on-platform payouts for large streamers. 9,523 of the 10,000 leaked records were matchable. The leak was never confirmed by Amazon but was corroborated by multiple streamers. Rank 10,000 of roughly 9.2 million streamers is approximately the top 0.11%. Spread over the ~26-month window, USD 23,520 is roughly USD 900 per month before tax and expenses (this monthly figure is arithmetic on the paper's numbers, not stated in the paper).
quoted_support: As to the remaining streamers in our final dataset, we find earnings ranging from 9.5 million US dollars down to 23,520$ only, providing a sense of the order of magnitude of the disparities in revenues.

claim: The weekly probability that a Twitch streamer drops out of the revenue ranking is about 0.2 for the top 100 and about 0.135 for the top 1,000, and more than 50% of streamers in the list were present from the very beginning of the observation window.
stance_target: That the creator elite turns over rapidly and that new entrants can readily displace incumbents — the 'anyone can make it' framing of creator careers.
scope_conditions: Iniguez et al. ranking-dynamics model applied to weekly Twitch revenue/viewership rankings, 2019-2021. Flux F is the probability an element present at T0 leaves at T1. Note the counterintuitive direction: lower-ranked positions churn MORE, higher-ranked positions less, and the authors attribute part of the top-100 vs top-1000 difference to list-size effects.
quoted_support: Specifically, the fitted models show that the probability of streamers in the list to drop below the threshold value for staying in the list at any round is about 0.2 for the top 100 and 0.13 for the top 1000 (Fig. 6). Moreover, in the supplementary plot, we can see that 50% of streamers in the list appear from the very early moments, and the higher the position in the list, the lower the probability of dropping out.

claim: Twitch's creator ranking is as stable as word-usage frequency in natural languages (flux 0.13-0.20) and far more stable than comparable social systems such as GitHub repositories (0.65) or Guardian readership (0.80).
stance_target: Creator success, once attained, is highly persistent, and the observed 'attrition' in creator populations occurs overwhelmingly below the visible elite rather than through elite displacement.
scope_conditions: Comparison of fitted ranking-flux parameters across datasets from Iniguez et al.'s original study. Twitch data 2019-2021.
quoted_support: Twitch top 100: F approximately 0.2; Twitch top 1000: F approximately 0.135; Society datasets (Guardian readers: F approximately 0.80; Github repositories: F approximately 0.65; Guardian commentaries: F approximately 0.61; Enron emails: F approximately 0.52); Language (word usage) datasets (French: F approximately 0.18; Russian: F approximately 0.18; Spanish: F approximately 0.16; Italian: F approximately 0.15; English: F approximately 0.13).

claim: Smaller Twitch streamers convert followers to paying subscribers more than twice as efficiently as the largest (0.017 subscribers per follower in the lowest revenue quintile versus 0.008 in the highest), and revenue scales sub-linearly with subscriber count (power-law exponent about 0.8).
stance_target: That top creators earn more because they monetize each audience member better — they do not; they earn more purely through volume and revenue diversification.
scope_conditions: Follower-to-subscriber conversion computed by revenue quintile within the top 10,000; subscriber counts from TwitchTracker as of February 2022 for the top 1,000. Spearman correlation between revenue and subscribers about 0.498 (p about 4.9e-56), R-squared of the power-law fit only about 0.38.
quoted_support: Furthermore it is easy to check that streamers with smaller revenues are relatively more able to convert non paying followers into paying subscribers (0.017 subscribers per follower for the lowest quintile against 0.008 for highest; see Supplementary Fig. 1).

claim: Top Twitch streamers carry substantially more sponsorship and affiliate links in their channel descriptions than lower-ranked or non-ranked streamers (average 3.7 for the top 2,000 versus 2.2 for a random sample outside the top 10,000).
stance_target: Off-platform income diversification is concentrated at the top, so leaked on-platform payout data understates total creator income inequality rather than overstating it.
scope_conditions: Sample of 1,333 streamers plus a random external sample of 330 active in May 2022; URL classification used a rudimentary keyword method. One-way ANOVA F approximately 44.2, p approximately 4.25e-11.
quoted_support: We see that the top 2000 streamers have an higher average (0-2000 approximately 3.7; 2000-4000 approximately 2.8; 4000-6000 approximately 2.4; 6000-8000 approximately 2.5; 8000-10,000 approximately 2.7; External sample approximately 2.2) as well as fatter tail distribution

claim: Twitch's average concurrent viewership more than doubled from 1.26 million in 2019 to 2.78 million in 2021, meaning the extreme measured inequality coexisted with rapid platform growth rather than with a shrinking pie.
stance_target: Rules out 'the market was contracting' as an explanation for concentration during the study window.
scope_conditions: Figures sourced from TwitchTracker aggregation of the Twitch API. Concurrent-viewer averages, not unique users.
quoted_support: Twitch gained much popularity during the Covid-19 pandemic, more than doubling the platform's audience from 1.26 million average concurrent viewers in 2019 to 2.78 million in 2021

claim: The leaked Twitch revenue figures cover only money flows from Amazon to streamers and therefore represent only part of actual streamer income.
stance_target: Bounds what the strongest available creator-income telemetry can and cannot establish.
scope_conditions: Author-stated limitation. Also: Amazon never confirmed the leak's accuracy, though multiple streamers corroborated their own figures; pseudonym drift between the leak and live platform data forced the authors to discard 477 of 10,000 records.
quoted_support: It is important to stress that the leaked data only consider the money flows received from Amazon, the Twitch parent company, and thus only represent a part of the streamers' actual revenues.
